title: Your seva, chosen
hookLine: write down the service you will keep
tomorrow: Maya's going to a different college. so who's Simran's sangat now?

lines: THE GURDWARA IS A LONG DRIVE.
cards: Simran's hands still smell faintly of onions from Sunday's langar kitchen, no matter how much soap she uses. She's got the campus map open, searching for the nearest gurdwara. It's a long drive, and she won't have a car.
So where does the seva go? She looks down at her hands on the phone. It goes where they go.

teach.b: Seva is service given freely, and in Sikh life it's mostly done with the hands.
Listen to it for a second: onions hissing in a huge pot, the clatter of steel plates being washed, the squeak of a mop on the langar floor.
At the gurdwara door, someone sits minding a wall of shoes, and that's seva too, often done by people you'd never expect to see doing it.
Guru Nanak puts it simply on Ang 26, paraphrased: serve here, in this world, and you'll be given a seat in the Lord's court. Notice the address. In this world.
Not only inside a gurdwara. So Simran makes her list with her hands, not a calendar.

teach.h: A PANTRY, A DOOR, A MONTHLY RIDE.
teach.b: Saturday mornings at a food pantry near campus, packing boxes. Holding the door for the roommate she hasn't met, carrying her boxes up the stairs on move-in day.
And the gurdwara once a month, when she can get a ride, back in the kitchen with the onions. Here's the detail worth passing on: in the langar kitchen nobody hands you a title.
You get a ladle, or a sponge, or a pile of shoes.

how: Sikhs do seva at the gurdwara by cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning and minding shoes, and outside it by serving neighbors, volunteering and helping after disasters, given freely.

o: the duty to read the Granth aloud in turns
the service you choose to keep, done with your hands
a fee paid to the gurdwara for its upkeep each year

games.q: seva, by hand — tap the pairs.
p: serve in this world, find a seat
minding the shoes at the door

s: seva only counts inside a gurdwara
Ang 26 says serve in this world. the gurdwara kitchen is one place among many.
Guru Nanak links serving in the world to a seat in the Lord's court
Ang 26, paraphrased: serve here, and you'll be given a seat.
in the langar kitchen, important people get the easier jobs
nobody hands you a title: you get a ladle, a sponge or a pile of shoes.

games.q: move-in day: the girl down the hall is drowning in boxes and you have a free hour. what does seva look like right now?
o: grab a box and carry it up with her, no fuss and no credit.
wait for an organized volunteer event; seva means a proper project.
post that you helped, so others feel inspired to help too.
games.why: seva is service given freely with your hands, in this world, as Ang 26 says. it doesn't need an event or an audience.

practice: Look at your hands for a slow minute: the knuckles, the lines, whatever they carried today. Then, with those same hands, write down the seva you'll keep: what, where and how often.
Keep it small enough that a hard week can't knock it over.

wordCard.voice: Your seva: the service you choose to keep, given freely and done with your own hands, wherever you are.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: selfless service, given freely, often with the hands.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: my seva goes where my hands go. Simran's list now has a food pantry on it.

sources.ref: Ang 26, Sri Rag, Guru Nanak ('vich duniaa sev kamaaeeai, taa dargah baisan paaeeai'), paraphrased
